titulo.texto: Panel with Stepped Frets in the Mitla Style

frase_gancho.texto: A wall of thousands of stones forming an endless labyrinth.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave the walls of Mitla behind to enter a royal tomb at Zaachila. Look for a tiny cup of polished clay in vivid colors, with a little bird modeled on the rim.

guion_corto.texto: This panel reproduces the stone mosaics of Mitla, a religious city of the Zapotec and the Mixtec. Mitla means “place of the dead” in Nahuatl, Mictlán, and in Zapotec Lyobaa, “place of rest.” What is astonishing is how it was made: it is not carved from a single block, but assembled from thousands of small, polished stones, fitted together one by one like a puzzle. With them, the stepped fret is formed, or xicalcoliuhqui, a design of lines that turn and fold. It has been interpreted as the serpent, storm clouds, the wind, or the path of souls. It measures almost two meters long and was designed to cover an entire wall.

guion_largo.texto:
There are places where architecture is a book. At Mitla it is a woven fabric. The palaces of this city were covered with stone mosaics that look like cloth, with lines that fold, step, and return upon themselves, so that no one can say where they begin or where they end. What you see here is one of those panels.

Let us begin with the name. Mitla comes from Mictlán, the Nahuatl word for the underworld, the “place of the dead,” to which, as you will remember, dogs accompanied their owners on their journey. In Zapotec the city was called Lyobaa, which is usually translated as “place of rest.” Two words to say the same thing: a place where one rests. It was considered a religious center of enormous importance, and it is thought that the Zapotec high priest lived there and that great lords were buried there.

Mitla flourished when Monte Albán had already lost its role as a capital, in the Postclassic, and it is above all the work of the Zapotec, with a Mixtec presence. The architects of Mitla invented a style of their own: instead of sculpting the walls, they covered them with mosaics made of thousands of pieces.

Come closer to the panel. It is not carved from a single block. Each piece was cut before being set in place and fitted against the others with a precision that leaves the joints almost invisible. It is as if, instead of painting or sculpting, they had woven with stone. It took a great deal of time, but the effect is unique: a surface that seems to vibrate with the light.

The design is called the stepped fret, and the Nahua Peoples knew it as xicalcoliuhqui, something like “twisted gourd bowl.” What does it mean? There is no single answer. It has been interpreted as the undulating body of a serpent, as storm clouds, as lightning, as the wind, and also as the winding path that souls travel to descend to the underworld. Perhaps all the readings are true at once: a design that offers more than one meaning, like a poem.

This fret is still alive. Zapotec weavers today repeat these designs on rugs, shawls, and tablecloths, and you have seen them, without knowing it, on thousands of Mexican objects. When you go up to the halls upstairs, you may recognize those same lines in today’s textiles. This is how you know a design is good: when it survives for centuries without needing an explanation.

There is one last historical irony. At Mitla, the Spaniards built a church, the Church of San Pablo, on top of an ancient palace, and reused its stones. Today, the church and the frets live side by side in the same place, like two eras layered on one another. And there is a local tradition: in the Hall of the Columns, it is said that whoever hugs the great central column and measures how far apart their hands are discovers how many years of life they have left. It is a legend, of course, but it says a lot about the site’s fame as a place of death and destiny.

With Mitla, death and art go hand in hand once again, as at the beginning of the hall. From [the Danzantes](mna_s07_danzante_montealban) to Mitla, passing through tombs, jades, and skulls, the peoples of Oaxaca thought of death not as an end, but as a place where one rests, waits, and is remembered. And they made it so beautiful that you still stop to look at it.

texto: Follow one of the lines of the fret with your eyes: does it end or does it continue?
Notice the joints between the stones: can you make them out?
Look for figures in the design: a serpent, a cloud, a lightning bolt?

texto.Material: Stone mosaic, polished limestone and volcanic tuff, pressed into place

texto.pregunta: Myth: The frets of Mitla are simple decorations.
texto.respuesta: Reality: For those who made them, they were symbols charged with meaning: they have been read as a serpent, a cloud, the wind, or the path of souls.
